title: PRD: Progressive compatibility plan for streaming-first SDKs (Python/TS/Go) with cursor-shard pagination and observable retries
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Goal: Define a pragmatic, incremental PRD that unifies streaming semantics, cursor-based pagination for sharded backends, and deterministic retry behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. The intent is to provide a single observable contract that: (1) supports duplex/bi-directional streaming use cases, (2) makes pagination resilient when results are sharded across nodes (cursor-shard model), and (3) defines retry windows and idempotency for transient failures without exposing implementation-specific artifacts to customers.

Why now: Multiple customers building low-latency chat and real-time analytics have reported brittle client behavior when switching versions or after backend shard rebalances. Our current SDK behavior diverges between languages: TS returns partial streams that cannot be resumed, Python exposes low-level cursor tokens, and Go retries are opaque. This causes integration regressions and increased support load.

Outcome: Deliver language SDK changes (public surface, contract, and tests), an SDK compatibility matrix and a staged rollout plan that allows existing clients to opt-in to the new contract and instruments observability signals (retry_reason, resume_possible, shard_id) for debugging and cost analysis.
scope: In-scope: 1) New public client APIs for streaming and pagination across Python/TS/Go with a consistent naming and error model; 2) Cursor-shard pagination format (opaque token containing position + shard fingerprint) and server-side hints for client backoff; 3) Deterministic retry rules and idempotency keys for fetch/append operations; 4) Cross-SDK conformance test suite and CI gating; 5) Migration guide and opt-in feature flag for existing clients.
out_of_scope: Out-of-scope: 1) Server-side shard rebalancing algorithms; 2) Deep runtime optimizations (batching kernels) — those are tracked by ENG; 3) Auto-paging helpers in high-level frameworks (will be a follow-up UX library deliverable).
acceptance_criteria: Public SDK surface parity: Python, TypeScript, and Go expose equivalent streaming primitives (StartStream, SendEvent/SendChunk, OnEvent/OnChunk, CloseStream) and a Pagination.Cursor type documented in SDK reference.
Cursor-shard token is opaque and stable across SDK versions: token roundtrip tests pass across language SDKs and with 3 different backend shard topologies.

Resume semantics: a stream interrupted with a transient network error can be resumed when server indicates resume_possible=true; client unit & integration tests demonstrate resume within configured window (default 30s).

Retry determinism: SDK retry policy yields identical request ordering and idempotency-key usage across languages for the same retryable error classes; conformance harness asserts request idempotency and no duplicate side-effects in 1000 randomized trials.

Observability: SDKs emit structured telemetry fields (retry_reason, retry_count, resume_attempted, shard_id_hint) to the Console debug endpoint; sample dashboards show per-route retry rate and resume success rate.

Backward compatibility: Existing clients remain functional with default settings; opt-in header `X-Redwood-SDK-Streaming-V2: true` enables new behavior. Regression tests ensure legacy requests return unchanged payload shape unless opt-in is present.
Documentation & migrations: PRD-linked migration guide and three language-specific cookbooks published (Python/TS/Go) with code examples and recommended default configs.
Security review: KMS usage for idempotency keys and cursor token encryption reviewed and approved by Security (security_review_required = true).
decisions: Use opaque base64 cursor that encodes (logical_offset, shard_fingerprint, server_epoch) to guard against client-side interpretation.
Expose resume_possible flag from the server; clients must not attempt to resume beyond a 30s default window unless configured by user.

Standardize retryable error classification across SDKs: NETWORK, THROTTLE, TRANSIENT_SERVER. Non-idempotent operations require explicit idempotency_key header, SDKs will surface helper to generate RFC-compliant keys.
Provide a single conformance test harness (node-based runner) that executes language bindings via thin adapters — tests declare expectations in YAML and assert via language-specific test runners.
Opt-in rollout: feature flag header to enable v2 behavior; GA after two cycles of opt-in telemetry showing <0.5% new-failure rate and resume success >95%.
Telemetry must be minimal by default; customers can opt into debug mode to surface resume traces and expanded retry_reason values.
Avoid automatic data migration for opaque tokens — server will accept legacy tokens and perform server-side translation when necessary to avoid invalidating existing clients.
notes: Trade-offs: Opaque tokens increase server-side decoding complexity but dramatically reduce client breakage from token schema drift.
We evaluated a purely stateless cursor (cursor = offset) but rejected it because sharded topologies can reorder offsets during rebalances leading to duplicate/skip behavior.
Alternate approach considered: explicit resume token exchange via a resume_endpoint. Rejected because it adds round-trip latency and complicates load balancers for low-latency streams.
Security: cursor will be HMAC-signed and optionally encrypted using KMS. Idempotency keys will be hashed client-side before transmission to avoid PII leakage.
